newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch brave cold and gloom for great skate race.
newsitem.headline: Dutch brave cold and gloom for great skate race.

text.p: More than 16,000 people braved darkness and bitter cold early on Saturday to embark on a legendary skating marathon over the frozen canals of the northern Dutch province of Friesland.

The 200-km (125-mile) Elfstedentocht (Eleven Cities Tour), held for only the 15th time this century, began at 0530 a.m. (0430 GMT). The winner was expected to finish around noon with the last contestants completing the course by midnight.

Tens of thousands of skating enthusiasts had poured into the Friesian capital of Leeuwarden and partied deep into the night to celebrate an event which is both a major sporting occasion and a national festival.
Hundreds of thousands were expected to converge along the route during the day, with some two-thirds of the 15 million Dutch people watching live television coverage of the race.

The Elfstedentocht, first held in 1909, acquired its legendary status because it can be held only when temperatures drop low enough to provide at least 15 cm (six inches) of ice along the entire course linking 11 mediaeval Friesian towns.
The competitive section of the race was being contested by an elite of 300 men and women who specialise in gruelling marathons held on natural ice in the depths of winter.
The winner will become a folk hero but his material rewards will be modest compared with those of professional sportsmen.
Evert van Benthem, winner of the last two races in 1985 and 1986, still works as a dairy farmer even though his name is known throughout the length and breadth of the Netherlands.
Most participants are driven by the simple honour of being able to take part and have no greater ambition than getting the medal given to everybody who finishes.
Over a quarter of this year's field were aged over 50, including 69-year-old Jeen van den Berg who won the race in 1954 and now hopes to complete the course for the seventh time.
Hundreds of race marshalls, police officers and first aid attendants were on duty, while hospitals prepared for an influx of casualties caused by frostbite, exhaustion and drunkenness.
